name: High lateral tension abdominoplasty

lead: High lateral tension (HLT) abdominoplasty is a variant of the tummy tuck described by plastic surgeon Ted Lockwood in the mid-1990s. Instead of pulling the skin mainly downward and tightening the centre, it removes extra skin from the sides and places the tightest closure along the lateral arms of the incision, with the superficial fascial system repaired in layers.

Surgeons who use it describe a more balanced contour of the waist and hips, a lower scar and reduced tension at the midline. It is often combined with liposuction of the trunk. Published work consists of surgeon-authored technique papers, a few comparative trials and case series.

paras: It is performed by a plastic surgeon under general anaesthesia, usually with a hip-to-hip incision, removal of excess skin and fat, repair of the superficial fascial system and, when needed, trunk liposuction. Recovery involves a period of limited activity and compression garments, with timelines set by the surgeon.

Abdominoplasty complications include seroma, haematoma, infection, wound separation, skin or fat necrosis, scarring, altered sensation, contour irregularities, blood clots and anaesthetic risks. Smoking, obesity, diabetes, prior abdominal surgery and combining procedures are listed as risk factors.

angle.text: The operation removes loose skin and fat from the abdomen and flanks and tightens the tissue so the torso looks flatter and the waist more defined. People seek it after pregnancy or large weight loss, or when exercise and diet have not changed loose skin.

lead: High lateral tension abdominoplasty (HLT) is a tummy-tuck technique built on the premise that the largest excess in the abdomen is usually at the sides, and that tightening the lateral tissue is what best improves the contour of the central abdomen [1][2]. The classic approach pulls the tissue downward and puts the highest tension on the central part of the incision; HLT pulls obliquely from the two lateral arms instead [2].

For looks, the goal is a flatter abdomen, a more defined waist and a scar sitting low and flat, achieved while limiting tension at the midline. Surgeons who developed the method reported it with superficial fascial system suspension and truncal liposuction [3][2]. It is one of the named types of abdominoplasty, alongside mini, extended, floating and circumferential variants [4].

paras: Modern abdominoplasty developed from the 1960s and typically removes excess skin and fat of the middle and lower abdomen while tightening the underlying fascia. HLT is listed among the recognised types and adds lateral tension vectors to vertical tightening, improving waist definition and reducing reliance on midline tension [4].

Key features described by the technique's author are limited direct undermining, increased lateral skin resection with highest-tension wound closure along the lateral limbs, two-layer superficial fascial system repair, and significant truncal liposuction when needed [2]. The author argues the design addresses practical and theoretical faults of standard abdominoplasty such as a high-riding scar, persistent fullness at the hips and flanks, and midline wound problems [5].

The method was introduced in a 1995 paper describing high-lateral-tension abdominoplasty with superficial fascial system suspension, a year before a 1996 plastic surgery comment on the technique [3][6]. Lockwood later described a lower-body lift built on the technique with a transverse thigh and buttock lift, which he developed in 1996 [7]. Further papers refined the approach, including a 2006 clarification and a 2010 update titled High tension abdominoplasty 2.0 [1][5].

The extended abdominoplasty lengthens the incision toward the posterior axillary line to remove lateral hip tissue [8]. A comparative trial of classic HLT and triangular resection looked at preventing dog ears and elongated scars [9]. A randomised study of 36 women compared laser-assisted liposuction with traditional liposuction combined with HLT abdominoplasty [10].

Abdominoplasty overall has a higher complication rate than many other cosmetic procedures because of the extent of dissection and tension. Listed complications include seroma, haematoma, infection, delayed healing, necrosis, scarring, sensation changes, asymmetry, thromboembolism and anaesthetic complications. Smoking, obesity, diabetes, prior surgery and combined procedures raise risk [4].

Evidence is mostly surgeon case series and technique papers. A randomised trial of 36 women compared laser-assisted and traditional liposuction combined with HLT abdominoplasty for effectiveness and safety [10]. A randomised open-label trial of 70 patients compared classic HLT with a triangular resection method for preventing dog ears and elongated scars [9].
